abstract: Humans and other animals develop rich visual representations without explicit object-category labels. Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a computational framework for studying how such representations emerge from visual experience. Many contrastive SSL models, such as SimCLR, learn by being robust to augmented views of the same image, which may fail to preserve visual attributes such as color and orientation. Inspired by feature-specific visual processing streams in the brain, we propose BioCLR, an SSL framework that uses color- and orientation-biased networks to guide representation learning. We combine Bio-CLR with SimCLR into a BioCLR hybrid model, pretrain it on ImageNet-100, and evaluate it on this dataset and four transfer datasets. In frozen linear evaluation, the BioCLR hybrid outperforms SimCLR across all datasets and mitigates negative transfer on a handwritten-character dataset. In limited-label fine-tuning, it outperforms SimCLR in most transfer conditions. Compared with the AugSelf and RotNet hybrids, which incorporate color and orientation information into SimCLR in other ways, the BioCLR hybrid shows the best overall performance, particularly in limited-label fine-tuning. Ablation analyses suggest that orientation guidance helps more than color guidance on these datasets, and that combining both generally improves frozen linear evaluation performance. Together, these findings suggest that incorporating feature-specific information into SSL can improve representation quality and model adaptability, and that the learning mechanism used to incorporate this information matters. For neuroscience, these results suggest that specialized visual streams in the brain may provide learning signals that guide visual representation learning without explicit supervision. For machine learning, they imply that principles of feature-biased processing in visual cortex may improve SSL.
